newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Iacocca in Taiwan electric bike venture.
newsitem.headline: Iacocca in Taiwan electric bike venture.

text.p: Like the carmarker he twice brought back from the dead, former Chrysler Corp. chief Lee Iacocca has found new life in wheeled transport.
But his new passion has only half as many wheels as a Chrysler, weighs far less and doesn't burn gasoline.
Iacocca wants to build electric bicycles in Taiwan.

During several days in Taiwan, the retired car exective signed letters of intent with Taiwan's Giant Co., one of the world's top bicycle makers, and UQM Electric Co. to make electric vehicles, executives said Wednesday.
Before leaving Taiwan on Tuesday, Iacocca told reporters he was confident his electric bicycle, manufactured by Giant, would hit the market in June 1998.
Taiwan's United Daily News said Giant would put $1 million into the venture under a letter of intent signed by Iacocca and Giant chairman Liu Chin-piao.
A Giant spokeswoman declined to confirm the figure, saying that investment amounts had not been discussed.

Separately, UQM Electric and Iacocca's EV Global Motors agreed to forge a strategic alliance to develop and market electric vehicles, said Wang Shuang-ching, president of Kwang Yang Motor, a major investor in UQM Electric.
The maverick American executive, who won fame for twice bringing Chrysler back from the brink of bankruptcy, retired from the carmaker in 1992 and formed EV Global in 1996.

The 72-year-old executive said environmentally friendly electric vehicles eventually would replace conventional gas-powered ones, but "not in my lifetime" because cheap, long-running batteries had yet to be developed.
If marketing of two-wheelers were successful, he could move on to electric automobiles, Iacocca said.
Giant executives said the bicycle-maker was eager to cooperate because electric vehicles would become a leading trend in the next century.
Kwang Yang's Wang said developing cost-efficient batteries was the key to the success of electric cars.
"Until now, we have yet to develop one that is both efficient and cheap," Wang said, predicting development could still take decades.
"But we still want to go forward because electric vehicles definitely will have a large market in the future."
